summary: Specifies a Telnet option that lets hosts exchange terminal speed information. Hosts that do so were expected to follow it. It was a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: When you connect to a faraway computer, it helps to know how fast your line is. This option lets your computer tell it.

subtitle: How Telnet hosts exchange the bit rate of the terminal on the other end.

tldr.problem: Operating systems use terminal speed for timing-dependent display work such as padding, but Telnet connections had no way to carry that information.
tldr.mechanism: The TERMINAL-SPEED option (code 32) is negotiated with WILL/DO, then the DO side sends a SEND request and the WILL side answers with an IS subcommand holding the transmit and receive speeds as text.
tldr.outcome: Hosts that exchange terminal speed within Telnet were expected to adopt this standard.

today: RFC 1079 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Terminal Speed Matters
sections.content:
Most operating systems keep track of the speed (bit rate) of directly attached terminals and modems. The information controls timing-dependent display processes, such as the number of padding characters used for delay, and some software tunes its interface for fast or slow terminals. This option provides the same information for Telnet connections.

The RFC is modelled on RFC 930, the Telnet terminal type option, and much of its text is copied from that RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: A slow screen needs pauses between letters. To add the right pauses, the computer must know the speed.

sections.title: Commands and Negotiation
sections.content:
The option is named TERMINAL-SPEED with code 32. WILL means the sender is willing to send speed information, and DO means it is willing to receive it. The defaults are WON'T and DON'T, so no speed information is exchanged unless negotiated.

WILL and DO only grant permission for later discussion. The real exchange happens in subnegotiation. Only the sender of the DO may send requests, and only the sender of the WILL may transmit speed information. Speed may not be sent spontaneously, only in response to a request.
sections.plainLanguage: First they agree to talk about speed. Then one asks, and only the other one answers. Nobody blurts out the speed unasked.

sections.title: The SEND and IS Subcommands
sections.content:
A request is IAC SB TERMINAL-SPEED SEND IAC SE, where SEND has the code 1. The answer is IAC SB TERMINAL-SPEED IS ... IAC SE, where IS has the code 0.

The speed is an NVT ASCII string holding the decimal transmit and receive speeds separated by a comma, for example 9600,100. No leading zeros or extra characters such as spaces may be included. In the RFC's example, Host1 sends DO, Host2 answers WILL, Host1 sends SEND, and Host2 replies IS "1200,1200".
sections.plainLanguage: The answer is written as two numbers with a comma between them, like 1200,1200: how fast it sends and how fast it receives.

sections.title: Implementation Suggestions
sections.content: Many systems allow only certain discrete terminal speeds, so a received speed may not match any allowed value. The RFC suggests picking the nearest allowed speed, rounding in a safe direction. If the speed is used for padding, it is best to round up, since too much padding is better than too little.
sections.plainLanguage: If the exact speed is not on your list, pick a nearby one, and choose the slower side so the screen has enough time.
